native_result.query: How is the advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students related to Socioeconomic status levels?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: The Black-vs-non-Black college-attendance gap in NLSY79 is SES-dependent in a widening pattern: near parity at low SES (3.4% vs 3.7%, −0.3 pp), small non-significant gap at middle SES (5.0% vs 6.5%, −1.5 pp), and a large significant gap at high SES (8.4% vs 19.3%, −11.0 pp; odds ratio ~0.35 vs ~0.87 at low SES; race×SES interaction p≈0.001). SES translates into college attendance far more steeply for non-Black than Black youths, so the Black disadvantage grows with socioeconomic status. This is measured with a dorm/fraternity/sorority residence proxy (1981-1996), not verified BA completion; commuter students are missed, undercounting may be race/SES-differential, data are observational, unweighted, and complete-case.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded nls_raw.csv (12,686 x 61); cleaned invalid grade=95 and identified income topcodes (75,001 in 1979). 2) Outcome: ever-dorm proxy (residence code 3 in any wave 1981-1996). 3) SES composite tertiles from standardized 1979 parental education (max of mom/dad) + 1979 family income (mean of available components). 4) Complete-case primary (N=12,532); race x SES tertile rates with Wilson CIs and rate differences. 5) Logistic regression ever_dorm ~ black x SES_tertile + age + sex (additive + multiplicative interaction); sensitivities: Black vs non-Black-non-Hispanic, parental-ed-only SES, income-only SES, income-missing indicator, ASVAB-adjusted (post-treatment caveat). Artifacts: analysis/nls_ba_analysis.py, analysis/rates_by_race_ses.csv, analysis/model_summary.txt.

sub_hypo.relations: Race modifies the association between SES and ever having residence code 3 during 1981–1996. SES tertiles derive from the mean of available standardized components: maximum maternal/paternal education and 1979 family income. Attendance increases with SES in both racial groups, but more steeply among non-Black respondents, widening the Black disadvantage. Black-versus-non-Black odds ratios are approximately 0.87 at low SES and 0.35 at high SES; the race×SES interaction has p≈0.001. Logistic regression adjusts for age and sex, with additive and multiplicative interaction assessed.
